description: I’m Nidhi, an IT Project Manager and solo participant from Thunder Bay, Ontario. After experiencing the effects of this year’s wildfire season, I’m building Fireline Replay, a dashboard that combines NASA satellite hotspot data and uses SI to analyze wildfire activity & generate interactive maps and charts. I bring experience in software delivery, product planning, and analytics. I’m open to connecting with others skilled in GIS, AI, or data visualisation.
summary:
EarthPulse is an interactive NASA Earth observation explorer that helps users understand wildfire activity through real satellite data. Built for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, the platform focuses on fire hotspot intelligence while laying the foundation for broader Earth system trend analysis.
Using NASA FIRMS data from MODIS and VIIRS sensors, EarthPulse lets users explore near-real-time and historical thermal anomalies across the globe or in specific regions. A dedicated Thunder Bay explorer highlights local fire activity, reflecting firsthand experience of the 2026 wildfire season in Northwestern Ontario. Users can view hotspots on an interactive map, a 3D globe, and a fire activity calendar that shows patterns over time.
The platform aggregates observations into clear daily counts, supports timeline replay, and provides satellite imagery from NASA GIBS. An analysis workspace is included for comparisons between sensors, seasons, and peak activity periods. Super Intelligence capabilities are planned to generate plain-language insights from the data.
EarthPulse addresses the need for clearer, more accessible interpretation of satellite fire observations. By combining real NASA data with regional focus and future AI analysis, it aims to help communities, researchers, and decision-makers better understand changing fire patterns and their local impact.
details:
EarthPulse is an interactive web application that helps users explore and understand wildfire activity using real NASA satellite data. It pulls near-real-time and historical thermal anomaly observations from NASA FIRMS (MODIS and VIIRS sensors). Users can view hotspots on an interactive map, a 3D globe, and a fire activity calendar. The platform includes a dedicated Thunder Bay explorer, timeline replay, and NASA GIBS satellite imagery for visual context. An analysis workspace allows comparison of sensors, seasons, and peak activity periods. Super Intelligence features are planned to generate plain-language insights from the data.

Benefits and Intended Impact

EarthPulse makes complex satellite fire data more accessible and understandable. It helps communities, researchers, and decision-makers see where and when fire activity is occurring, identify patterns over time, and better understand regional fire behavior. The project prioritizes the fire detection module because of firsthand experience with the 2026 Thunder Bay wildfires and the need for clearer, faster information. The long-term vision is to expand into a full Earth System Trend Detector that combines fire, climate trends, and surface change analysis.

Tools, Coding Languages, Software & Hardware Used

•  Frontend and application logic built with JavaScript, HTML, and CSS

•  NASA FIRMS Area API and NASA GIBS imagery

•  Cloudflare Workers for backend data handling

•  GitHub for version control and hosting

•  CapCut and Muse for creating the demo video

•  ChatGPT and Claude used for vibe coding, debugging, and accelerating development

•  YouTube for hosting the project demo video

•  NASA Eyes and Earth research resources used as visual and conceptual references

Creativity and Design Considerations

The project combines scientific satellite data with a clean, interactive interface focused on usability. Creativity comes from turning raw thermal anomaly records into an explorable experience (map + globe + calendar + timeline) while keeping a clear path toward AI-powered insights. Key factors considered include data accuracy and limitations (thermal anomalies vs confirmed fires), regional relevance (Thunder Bay focus), accessibility for non-experts, and a modular design that allows future expansion into Earth trends and surface change detection.

Why I Created EarthPulse

I created EarthPulse after personally experiencing the 2026 Thunder Bay wildfires. The alerts were slow and the information available to the public was often unclear or delayed. I wanted to build a tool that turns complex NASA satellite data into something people can actually understand and use in real time.

The first priority was fire detection because that was the problem I lived through. Using NASA FIRMS data from MODIS and VIIRS, EarthPulse shows where thermal anomalies are occurring, how activity is changing over time, and provides a clearer picture for communities, researchers, and decision-makers.

Utilizing Super Intelligence

Super Intelligence is a core part of the vision. While the current version focuses on clean data exploration and visualization, the long-term plan is to integrate SI so the system can analyze patterns, explain what the data means in plain language, and answer natural questions.

By training the system on large volumes of Earth observation data (fire hotspots, climate trends, satellite imagery, and related environmental records), EarthPulse can evolve into a conversational Earth intelligence tool. Users will be able to ask questions such as:

•  “How does this year’s fire activity in Northwestern Ontario compare to the last 10 years?”

•  “What areas are showing unusual thermal patterns right now?”

•  “Is this trend significant?”

The goal is to move from simply displaying data to helping people understand and act on it.

Path to Commercial Use

Once Super Intelligence is fully integrated and trained on rich Earth datasets, EarthPulse can expand beyond a single-purpose fire tool into a broader commercial Earth intelligence platform. It could serve emergency managers, researchers, media, insurance companies, and the public by providing fast, reliable, and easy-to-understand answers about wildfires, environmental trends, and planetary change.

EarthPulse starts with a real problem experienced in Thunder Bay and grows into a system that makes Earth data more accessible, intelligent, and useful for everyone.
